## Motivation {#motivation}

A model can make accurate predictions on held-out training-style examples and still encounter different cases after deployment.
Training and deployment may expose a model to different distributions.
Identifying the changed distribution and the assumed causal relationships prevents several different issues from being called the same thing.

## Which distribution changes? {#distribution-shift}

Distribution shift is a relation between two probability distributions: the training distribution and the deployment distribution differ.
For supervised prediction, the relevant object is often the joint distribution of input $x$ and target $y$.
A finite dataset provides observations from a distribution; a difference between two finite samples alone does not prove that their underlying distributions differ.

Covariate shift is the more specific assumption that $p_{\mathrm{train}}(x)\ne p_{\mathrm{test}}(x)$ while $p(y\mid x)$ stays the same.
Here $p(x)$ is the input [marginal distribution]{.term key="marginal-distribution"}, whereas $p(y\mid x)$ is the target's [conditional distribution]{.term key="conditional-distribution"}.
A change in the full joint distribution alone does not establish that assumption.

For example, suppose training contains equal numbers of bright and dark scenes, while deployment contains mostly dark scenes.
If the target distribution for each given scene stays unchanged, this is a covariate-shift example.
If a changed labeling rule also changes the target for the same input, the stated covariate-shift assumption no longer holds.
These are hypotheses about the data-generating distributions, not conclusions established merely by observing a performance drop.

## Policy-induced observation shift {#policy-induced-shift}

In [behavioural cloning]{.term key="behavioural-cloning"}, the learner's actions affect which observations it later visits.
Errors can therefore move the learner away from the expert's training distribution.
[DAgger](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0686) addresses this by obtaining expert supervision on states induced by the learner.

## Confounding is a causal claim {#confounding}

A confounder, in a causal analysis, influences both a putative cause and an outcome and can create a misleading association between them.
For example, suppose a scene variable determines both the background colour and which task a demonstrator is assigned.
That scene variable can confound the association between background colour and demonstrated action; the colour itself is not automatically the confounder.
Correlation alone does not establish this causal structure.

## Internal activation changes {#internal-covariate-shift}

“Internal covariate shift” names the explanation proposed in the original [batch normalisation paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167).
Batch normalisation standardises activations using batch statistics and then applies a learned scale and shift, so final activations need not have mean zero or variance one.
[Santurkar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11604) provide evidence that smoother optimisation, rather than reduced internal distribution shift alone, is important to its effectiveness.

## Applications, connections, and boundaries {#connections}

When performance changes, first state which inputs and targets are being compared and how each dataset was collected.
Then separate evidence of changed distributions from the stronger claim that a particular causal mechanism explains the failure.
Distribution shift can occur without the background-variable confounding described above, and such confounding can persist even when the training and deployment distributions are the same.

[Behavioural cloning](../robotics/policies.qmd#policies) learns from demonstrated observations and actions, while the deployed policy helps determine its future observations.
[Action horizons and feedback](../robotics/action-horizons.qmd) describe when the controller can respond to those observations.
[Conditional and marginal distributions](../mathematics/probability.qmd#conditional-and-marginal) provide the notation needed to state a particular shift assumption.
